before.definition: A single random experiment with exactly two outcomes, success (probability p) and failure (probability 1 − p). Repeated independent Bernoulli trials underlie the binomial and geometric distributions.
before.example: Each packet sent over a link that drops 1% of packets is a Bernoulli trial with p = 0.01 for 'lost'.

after.definition: A random experiment with two labelled outcomes, success and failure. Independent repetitions with one common success probability underlie the binomial and geometric distributions; a single Bernoulli trial does not itself assert independence from other trials.
after.example: Each packet sent over a link that drops 1% of packets is a Bernoulli trial with p = 0.01 for 'lost'.

before.definition: The fraction of real positive cases that a test or detector correctly flags, P(positive result | real case). Called sensitivity in medicine and recall in machine learning.
before.example: A test that detects 99 of 100 ill people has sensitivity 99%.

after.definition: The fraction of real positive cases that a test or detector correctly flags, P(positive result | real case). Called sensitivity in medicine and recall in machine learning.
after.example: A test that detects 99 of 100 ill people has sensitivity 99%.

before.definition: In classification, the fraction of predicted positives that are really positive, P(actually positive | predicted positive). It is the Bayesian posterior of an alert, and, with sensitivity and false positive rate fixed, it falls as the base rate falls.
before.example: 980 real frauds among 10,970 alerts is a precision of about 8.9%.

after.definition: In classification, the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive, when positive predictions have nonzero probability. It depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and false-positive rate. With positive sensitivity and positive false-positive rate fixed, lowering prevalence lowers precision; zero false positives are an important exception.
after.example: 980 real frauds among 10,970 alerts is a precision of about 8.9%.

before.definition: The fraction of all predictions a classifier gets right. On imbalanced data it can be very high for a useless model, so precision and recall are reported instead.

after.definition: The fraction of all predictions a classifier gets right. On imbalanced data it can be very high for a useless model, so precision and recall are reported instead.

before.definition: A pair of positions in an array where the earlier element is larger than the later one. Insertion sort does one swap or shift per inversion; a random permutation has n(n − 1)/4 on average.

after.definition: A pair of array positions where the earlier value is larger than the later one. Adjacent-swap insertion sort uses one swap per inversion; the usual shifting version uses one rightward shift per inversion. For a uniformly random permutation of distinct values, each pair is inverted with probability one-half.

before.definition: The symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of it lies within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.

after.definition: A symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution specified by its mean and positive standard deviation. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% lies within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean; these are two-sided bands, not one-sided percentile labels.

before.definition: A value far from most of the others, such as one timed-out request among fast ones. It moves the mean a lot and the median hardly at all.

after.definition: An observation far from most of the others, such as one timeout among fast requests. Extreme observations can strongly influence the mean; the median is more resistant because it depends on central ranks rather than the magnitudes of tail observations.

lookups.definition: A random experiment with two labelled outcomes, success and failure. Independent repetitions with one common success probability underlie the binomial and geometric distributions; a single Bernoulli trial does not itself assert independence from other trials.
The fraction of real positive cases that a test or detector correctly flags, P(positive result | real case). Called sensitivity in medicine and recall in machine learning.

In classification, the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive, when positive predictions have nonzero probability. It depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and false-positive rate. With positive sensitivity and positive false-positive rate fixed, lowering prevalence lowers precision; zero false positives are an important exception.

The fraction of all predictions a classifier gets right. On imbalanced data it can be very high for a useless model, so precision and recall are reported instead.

A pair of array positions where the earlier value is larger than the later one. Adjacent-swap insertion sort uses one swap per inversion; the usual shifting version uses one rightward shift per inversion. For a uniformly random permutation of distinct values, each pair is inverted with probability one-half.

A symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution specified by its mean and positive standard deviation. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% lies within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean; these are two-sided bands, not one-sided percentile labels.

An observation far from most of the others, such as one timeout among fast requests. Extreme observations can strongly influence the mean; the median is more resistant because it depends on central ranks rather than the magnitudes of tail observations.
